## Secure Software Development

**Parent L1**: Application Security
**ADM Phase**: Phase A–B
**Description**: Secure Software Development is the organizational capability to embed security intent and validation into the software development lifecycle at the earliest feasible point. This capability ensures that security requirements are identified and addressed during design (through threat modeling and architecture review), that developers have access to secure coding guidance appropriate to their technology context, and that automated gates enforce minimum security posture before code advances in the pipeline. The outcome is software that is designed with attack resistance in mind rather than retrofitted after the fact.
**Strategic Alignment**: Supports the Protect and Identify functions of the NIST CSF 2.0; aligns to the enterprise principle of security by design.
**Zero Trust Relevance**: Advances the Applications and Workloads pillar of Zero Trust by ensuring applications are architected to assume untrusted execution environments and minimize implicit trust in their own components.
**Key Stakeholders**: Application Development Teams, Platform Engineering, Security Architecture, DevSecOps Practice
**Related ABBs**: [GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-SSDLC-2.7.25](./abbs/GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-SSDLC-2.7.25.md)
**Capability Boundary**: Does not cover automated security testing tooling (see Application Security Testing), API-specific security patterns (see API Security), or the security of build pipeline infrastructure itself (see Software Supply Chain Security).

## API Security

**Parent L1**: Application Security
**ADM Phase**: Phase B
**Description**: API Security is the capability to protect application programming interfaces across their full lifecycle — from design through deprecation. This capability governs how APIs are exposed to consumers (internal, partner, or public), how identity assertions and authorization decisions are enforced at API boundaries, how API traffic is mediated and validated, and how API inventories are maintained to prevent shadow API proliferation. The outcome is a consistent architectural pattern for API exposure that prevents unauthorized access and data leakage at the interface layer.
**Strategic Alignment**: Supports the Protect function of NIST CSF 2.0; directly enables Zero Trust API-to-API communication patterns.
**Zero Trust Relevance**: Central to the Applications and Workloads pillar — every API call is a trust decision that must be explicitly authorized, regardless of network location.
**Key Stakeholders**: Integration Architects, API Platform Teams, Security Architecture, Application Development Teams
**Related ABBs**: [GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-APIGW-2.7.11](./abbs/GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-APIGW-2.7.11.md), [GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-APIAZ-2.7.12](./abbs/GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-APIAZ-2.7.12.md)
**Capability Boundary**: Does not cover enterprise identity federation or workforce SSO (see Identity Security domain); does not cover network-layer traffic controls (see Network Security domain).

## Application Security Testing

**Parent L1**: Application Security
**ADM Phase**: Phase B
**Description**: Application Security Testing is the capability to systematically identify security weaknesses in application code, running application behavior, and third-party dependencies through automated analysis at appropriate stages of the development and deployment pipeline. This capability encompasses static code analysis (before execution), dynamic analysis (against running instances), interactive analysis (instrumented at runtime during testing), and software composition analysis (against dependency manifests). The architectural outcome is a layered testing posture that provides security visibility across the application at build, test, and pre-deployment gates.
**Strategic Alignment**: Supports the Identify and Detect functions of NIST CSF 2.0; foundational to shift-left security practice.
**Zero Trust Relevance**: Indirectly supports all Zero Trust pillars by reducing the exploitable attack surface of applications before they are deployed into trusted execution environments.
**Key Stakeholders**: DevSecOps Practice, Platform Engineering, Security Architecture, Application Development Teams
**Related ABBs**: [GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-SAST-2.7.07](./abbs/GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-SAST-2.7.07.md), [GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-DAST-2.7.08](./abbs/GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-DAST-2.7.08.md), [GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-IAST-2.7.09](./abbs/GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-IAST-2.7.09.md), [GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-SCA-2.7.10](./abbs/GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-SCA-2.7.10.md)
**Capability Boundary**: Does not cover penetration testing or red team exercises (these are operational security activities outside the development pipeline scope); does not cover infrastructure vulnerability scanning (see Cloud & Infrastructure Security domain).

## Container & Image Security

**Parent L1**: Application Security
**ADM Phase**: Phase B
**Description**: Container & Image Security is the capability to ensure that container images are free from known vulnerabilities and policy violations from the point of build, that their provenance and integrity can be attested through the supply chain, and that their runtime behavior is constrained to their declared purpose. This capability addresses the security concerns unique to the container packaging model — including base image hygiene, build-time scanning, image signing, and behavioral constraints applied when a container is instantiated. The architectural outcome is a secure-by-default container lifecycle that prevents compromised or misconfigured images from reaching production.
**Strategic Alignment**: Supports the Protect function of NIST CSF 2.0; enables supply chain integrity principles.
**Zero Trust Relevance**: Advances the Applications and Workloads pillar — containers are workload execution units whose identity and integrity must be verified before trust is extended.
**Key Stakeholders**: Platform Engineering, DevSecOps Practice, Security Architecture
**Related ABBs**: [GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-IMGSC-2.7.13](./abbs/GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-IMGSC-2.7.13.md), [GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-RTCON-2.7.14](./abbs/GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-RTCON-2.7.14.md)
**Capability Boundary**: Does not cover orchestration-layer policy enforcement (see Container Orchestration Security); does not cover the security of the registry infrastructure itself (see Cloud & Infrastructure Security domain).

[strategy/guidance/security/Application/GUID-SEC-APP-CAP-DESC-1.7.02.md#container-orchestration-security]

## Container Orchestration Security

**Parent L1**: Application Security
**ADM Phase**: Phase B
**Description**: Container Orchestration Security is the capability to establish and maintain a secure configuration posture for container orchestration platforms — principally the control plane, workload scheduling, inter-pod network policy, and role-based access controls that govern how containerized workloads are deployed and operated at scale. This capability is concerned with the security of the orchestration layer as a platform, distinct from the security of the individual container images it manages. The architectural outcome is an orchestration environment that enforces least-privilege workload deployment, isolates workloads from one another, and protects the control plane from unauthorized access.
**Strategic Alignment**: Supports the Protect function of NIST CSF 2.0; enables Zero Trust workload isolation.
**Zero Trust Relevance**: Directly advances the Applications and Workloads and Networks pillars — the orchestration platform is the enforcement point for workload identity and network segmentation at the compute layer.
**Key Stakeholders**: Platform Engineering, Cloud Infrastructure Teams, Security Architecture
**Related ABBs**: [GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-K8SRBAC-2.7.15](./abbs/GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-K8SRBAC-2.7.15.md), [GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-K8SCP-2.7.16](./abbs/GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-K8SCP-2.7.16.md)
**Capability Boundary**: Does not cover node/host OS hardening (see Cloud & Infrastructure Security domain); does not cover container image scanning (see Container & Image Security).

## Database Security

**Parent L1**: Application Security
**ADM Phase**: Phase B
**Description**: Database Security is the capability to protect data stored within enterprise database systems through architectural controls that govern how access to data is requested, authorized, and audited at the database tier. This capability encompasses the architectural patterns for database access control, the monitoring of database activity for anomalous or unauthorized behavior, and the confidentiality of data at rest within database storage. It is concerned with the database as an application-tier asset — distinct from enterprise data governance or data classification, which operate at a higher abstraction level. The architectural outcome is a database tier where access is controlled, activity is visible, and data confidentiality is maintained through consistent architectural patterns.
**Strategic Alignment**: Supports the Protect and Detect functions of NIST CSF 2.0; essential for healthcare data protection obligations.
**Zero Trust Relevance**: Advances the Data pillar of Zero Trust — data access at the database tier must be authorized on a per-request basis with full audit visibility.
**Key Stakeholders**: Database Administrators, Application Development Teams, Security Architecture, Compliance
**Related ABBs**: [GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-DAM-2.7.17](./abbs/GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-DAM-2.7.17.md), [GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-DBENC-2.7.18](./abbs/GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-DBENC-2.7.18.md)
**Capability Boundary**: Does not cover enterprise data classification or data lifecycle management (see Data Security domain); does not cover database infrastructure provisioning or patching (see Cloud & Infrastructure Security domain).

[strategy/guidance/security/Application/GUID-SEC-APP-CAP-DESC-1.7.02.md#web-application-protection]

## Web Application Protection

**Parent L1**: Application Security
**ADM Phase**: Phase B
**Description**: Web Application Protection is the capability to defend application-layer endpoints from exploitation at runtime — after the application has been deployed and is actively serving traffic. This capability addresses the architectural need to inspect, filter, and respond to malicious or anomalous requests targeting web application endpoints, and to detect and prevent exploitation attempts from within the application process itself. It is a runtime defense capability, complementary to but distinct from pre-deployment testing (Application Security Testing). The architectural outcome is a runtime defense posture that reduces the exploitability of deployed applications even in the presence of unpatched vulnerabilities.
**Strategic Alignment**: Supports the Protect and Detect functions of NIST CSF 2.0; provides defense-in-depth at the application runtime layer.
**Zero Trust Relevance**: Advances the Applications and Workloads pillar — runtime protection mechanisms enforce the assumption that the application environment cannot be fully trusted.
**Key Stakeholders**: Application Operations Teams, Platform Engineering, Security Architecture
**Related ABBs**: [GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-WAF-2.7.19](./abbs/GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-WAF-2.7.19.md), [GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-RASP-2.7.20](./abbs/GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-RASP-2.7.20.md)
**Capability Boundary**: Does not cover network-layer DDoS mitigation (see Network Security domain); does not cover pre-deployment vulnerability identification (see Application Security Testing).

[strategy/guidance/security/Application/GUID-SEC-APP-CAP-DESC-1.7.02.md#application-authentication--authorization]

## Application Authentication & Authorization

**Parent L1**: Application Security
**ADM Phase**: Phase B
**Description**: Application Authentication & Authorization is the capability to establish and enforce identity assertions and access decisions within and between application components — at the application layer. This capability addresses the architectural patterns by which applications verify the identity of callers (authentication), determine what actions those callers are permitted to perform (authorization), and manage the tokens and assertions that carry those decisions across service boundaries. It is distinct from enterprise identity governance (which manages the workforce identity lifecycle) and focuses on the application-layer trust model — including service-to-service authentication and fine-grained authorization within application logic. The architectural outcome is an application landscape where every request carries a verifiable identity and is subject to explicit authorization.
**Strategic Alignment**: Supports the Protect function of NIST CSF 2.0; foundational to Zero Trust application access.
**Zero Trust Relevance**: Central to the Identity and Applications and Workloads pillars — no implicit trust in application-to-application calls; every assertion must be validated.
**Key Stakeholders**: Application Development Teams, Integration Architects, Security Architecture, Identity & Access Management Teams
**Related ABBs**: [GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-IDBRKR-2.7.26](./abbs/GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-IDBRKR-2.7.26.md), [GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-TOKVAL-2.7.27](./abbs/GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-TOKVAL-2.7.27.md)
**Capability Boundary**: Does not cover enterprise workforce identity management, directory services, or SSO federation (see Identity Security domain); does not cover API gateway-level authentication enforcement (see API Security).

[strategy/guidance/security/Application/GUID-SEC-APP-CAP-DESC-1.7.02.md#secrets-management]

## Secrets Management

**Parent L1**: Application Security
**ADM Phase**: Phase B
**Description**: Secrets Management is the capability to govern the full lifecycle of application credentials, cryptographic keys, API tokens, certificates, and other sensitive configuration values that applications require to authenticate to services, encrypt data, or invoke privileged operations. This capability addresses the architectural need to store secrets securely (never in source code or unencrypted configuration), distribute them to applications through controlled mechanisms, enforce access policies on their retrieval, and rotate them on a defined schedule or in response to a compromise event. The architectural outcome is an application landscape where secrets are never exposed in plaintext outside of authorized, audited access paths.
**Strategic Alignment**: Supports the Protect function of NIST CSF 2.0; directly enables Zero Trust credential hygiene.
**Zero Trust Relevance**: Advances the Identity and Data pillars — secrets are identity material and must be protected with the same rigor as user credentials.
**Key Stakeholders**: Application Development Teams, Platform Engineering, Security Architecture, Cloud Infrastructure Teams
**Related ABBs**: [GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-VAULT-2.7.21](./abbs/GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-VAULT-2.7.21.md), [GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-DSECR-2.7.22](./abbs/GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-DSECR-2.7.22.md)
**Capability Boundary**: Does not cover enterprise PKI or certificate authority operations (see Infrastructure Security domain); does not cover key management for data-at-rest encryption at the platform level (see Cloud & Infrastructure Security domain).

page_texts.12:
[strategy/guidance/security/Application/GUID-SEC-APP-CAP-DESC-1.7.02.md#software-supply-chain-security]

## Software Supply Chain Security

**Parent L1**: Application Security
**ADM Phase**: Phase A–B
**Description**: Software Supply Chain Security is the capability to establish and maintain confidence in the integrity and provenance of all software components, build artifacts, and external dependencies that constitute an enterprise application. This capability addresses the architectural risk that software delivered to production may contain components whose origin, integrity, or vulnerability status cannot be verified — whether through compromised dependencies, tampered build pipelines, or untracked transitive inclusions. The architectural outcomes are: a maintained inventory of all software components (SBOM), verified integrity of build artifacts at each pipeline stage, and the ability to identify and respond to supply chain compromise events. This is an emerging capability for the enterprise and reflects the increasing recognition of supply chain risk as a primary attack vector.
**Strategic Alignment**: Supports the Identify and Protect functions of NIST CSF 2.0; directly responsive to executive-level guidance on software supply chain risk.
**Zero Trust Relevance**: Advances the Applications and Workloads pillar — software provenance is an aspect of workload identity; unverified components represent an implicit trust assumption that Zero Trust architecture rejects.
**Key Stakeholders**: DevSecOps Practice, Platform Engineering, Security Architecture, Procurement/Vendor Management
**Related ABBs**: [GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-SBOM-2.7.23](./abbs/GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-SBOM-2.7.23.md), [GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-DEPINT-2.7.24](./abbs/GUID-SEC-APP-ABB-DEPINT-2.7.24.md)
**Capability Boundary**: Does not cover vendor security assessments or third-party risk management (see Governance, Risk & Compliance domain); does not cover the security of build infrastructure itself (see Cloud & Infrastructure Security domain).
